label: Extremely Low Frequency
description: ELF waves (3–30 Hz) penetrate seawater to great depths, making them uniquely suited for communicating with submerged submarines. They also arise naturally from lightning discharges in the Earth-ionosphere cavity, a phenomenon known as Schumann resonances.
interactions: travels around Earth via Earth-ionosphere waveguide
hazards: extremely low-level power-line fields studied for biological effects, no confirmed hazard at environmental levels

label: Super Low Frequency
description: SLF waves (30–300 Hz) overlap with power-line frequencies and penetrate even deeper into seawater than ELF. The US Navy operated SLF transmitters in Wisconsin and Michigan for strategic submarine communications during the Cold War.
interactions: penetrates seawater to several hundred meters
induces eddy currents in conductive ground
hazards: occupational exposure near high-power transmitters studied; no confirmed carcinogenic effect at permitted levels

label: Ultra Low Frequency
description: ULF waves (300 Hz–3 kHz) propagate through the Earth and rock formations, enabling communication in mines and underground facilities. They are also associated with geomagnetic pulsations generated by solar wind interactions with Earth's magnetosphere.
hazards: no established hazard at environmental levels

label: Very Low Frequency
description: VLF waves (3–30 kHz) propagate globally inside the Earth-ionosphere waveguide with very low attenuation, enabling worldwide navigation and time signals. The OMEGA navigation system operated in VLF until 1997; military VLF stations still communicate with submarines.
hazards: no established hazard at environmental levels

label: Low Frequency
description: LF waves (30–300 kHz) support AM longwave broadcasting in Europe and Asia, and ground-wave propagation follows the Earth's curvature for hundreds of kilometers. LORAN-C (100 kHz) and NDB (non-directional beacons) used LF for maritime and aviation navigation.
interactions: skywave at night via ionospheric reflection
hazards: no established hazard at environmental levels

label: Medium Frequency
description: MF waves (300 kHz–3 MHz) carry AM broadcast radio (530–1700 kHz in North America) via ground wave during the day and ionospheric skywave at night. The international maritime distress frequency 2182 kHz lies in MF, and the 160m amateur band occupies 1.8–2.0 MHz.
interactions: D-layer absorption by day, E-layer reflection at night
applications: AM broadcast radio (530–1700 kHz NTSC, 153–1602 kHz ITU)
hazards: no established hazard at environmental levels

label: High Frequency (Shortwave)
description: HF waves (3–30 MHz) refract off the ionospheric F-layer, enabling intercontinental radio communication without satellites. Shortwave broadcasting, amateur radio (ham), CB radio, and NVIS military communication all operate in HF. Skip distance and propagation depend heavily on solar conditions.
interactions: F-layer ionospheric refraction for transoceanic skip
hazards: no established hazard at environmental levels

label: Very High Frequency
description: VHF (30–300 MHz) supports FM radio, television (channels 2–13), aviation communications, and NOAA weather radio. Propagation is line-of-sight with occasional troposcatter and sporadic-E enhancement. FM radio occupies 87.5–108 MHz; aviation uses 108–137 MHz (VOR/ILS and comms).
applications: aviation (108–137 MHz: VOR, ILS, ATIS, comms)
hazards: no established hazard at environmental levels

label: Ultra High Frequency
description: UHF (300 MHz–3 GHz) is the most congested part of the spectrum, hosting cellular networks, WiFi 2.4 GHz, Bluetooth, GPS, digital TV, and microwave ovens. Line-of-sight propagation with significant building penetration. GPS signals arrive at 1.575 GHz (L1) and 1.227 GHz (L2).
interactions: atmospheric oxygen absorption near 60 GHz edge
hazards: SAR (Specific Absorption Rate) limits enforced for mobile phones; non-ionizing at typical exposure levels

label: Super High Frequency
description: SHF (3–30 GHz) hosts WiFi 5/6 GHz, satellite downlinks (Ku-band 12–18 GHz), weather radar, and the emerging 5G mmWave bands (24–40 GHz). Rain attenuation becomes significant above 10 GHz. Directional antennas are compact at these wavelengths.
interactions: oxygen absorption at 22 GHz water vapor line
applications: satellite Ku-band (11.7–12.7 GHz down, 14.0–14.5 GHz up)
weather radar C-band (5.6 GHz) and X-band (9.6 GHz)
hazards: non-ionizing; SAR limits apply to devices held near body; high-power radar beams hazardous at close range

label: Extremely High Frequency (mmWave)
description: EHF/mmWave (30–300 GHz) features severe atmospheric attenuation with windows at 35, 94, 140, and 220 GHz. The 60 GHz band has 15 dB/km oxygen absorption, enabling dense frequency reuse. Automotive radar at 77 GHz enables adaptive cruise control and collision avoidance.
interactions: rain attenuation up to 10 dB/km at 100 GHz
high-resolution radar due to short wavelength
short propagation range enables dense frequency reuse
hazards: surface heating of skin and eye cornea at high power levels; non-ionizing

label: Submillimeter / Terahertz Gap
description: Submillimeter waves (300 GHz–3 THz) straddle the boundary between microwave and infrared. Strong atmospheric water vapor absorption limits terrestrial propagation. Terahertz imaging can see through clothing and packaging, and molecular rotational spectroscopy uses this band extensively.
hazards: surface heating; no ionization; research ongoing into biological effects

label: Far Infrared
description: Far IR (3–30 THz, 10–100 μm) is dominated by thermal emission from room-temperature objects and molecular vibrational-rotational transitions. The Earth's atmosphere emits strongly in this band, and astronomers observe it from high-altitude or space observatories. CO2 laser emission at 10.6 μm is in the far IR boundary.
interactions: absorbed by atmospheric water vapor and CO2
emitted by all objects at room temperature (300 K peak ~10 μm)
Reststrahlen band absorption in ionic crystals
applications: thermal imaging cameras (8–14 μm atmospheric window)
CO2 laser surgery and cutting (10.6 μm)
hazards: skin burns from high-power far-IR lasers; non-ionizing

label: Mid Infrared
description: Mid IR (30–120 THz, 2.5–10 μm) contains fundamental molecular vibrational absorption bands used as chemical 'fingerprints' in spectroscopy. The 3–5 μm and 8–14 μm atmospheric windows are used for thermal imaging and heat-seeking missiles. Quantum cascade lasers cover this entire band.
interactions: atmospheric windows at 3–5 μm and 8–14 μm
high sensitivity to hydrocarbons and gases
solar absorption by CO2 and H2O greenhouse effect
applications: FLIR thermal cameras (3–5 μm and 8–12 μm)
heat-seeking missile seekers (4.2 μm CO2 plume)
hazards: thermal burns from high-power pulsed lasers; corneal damage from IR lasers

label: Near Infrared
description: Near IR (120–430 THz, 700 nm–2500 nm) is used extensively in fiber-optic telecommunications (1310 nm and 1550 nm telecom windows), night vision, remote controls (940 nm), and medical imaging. Silicon photodetectors are sensitive to ~1100 nm; InGaAs extends coverage to 1700 nm.
interactions: transmitted by silica glass fiber (1310 nm, 1550 nm windows)
penetrates biological tissue 1–3 cm (optical window 700–1000 nm)
applications: fiber-optic telecommunications (1310 nm SMF, 1550 nm DWDM)
night vision devices (Gen I–III image intensifiers)
hazards: retinal burns from high-power near-IR lasers (eye does not blink reflex); Class 3B and 4 laser hazards
sources: laser diodes (780 nm DVD, 808 nm pump, 1550 nm telecom)

label: Violet Light
description: Violet (380–450 nm) is at the short-wavelength edge of human vision, perceived by the S-cone photoreceptors. It scatters strongly in the atmosphere (Rayleigh scattering ∝ λ⁻⁴), contributing to the blue sky. GaN-based LEDs and violet laser diodes (405 nm) are widely used in Blu-ray players and fluorescence microscopy.
interactions: absorbed by the eye lens (crystalline lens yellows with age)
hazards: prolonged exposure can contribute to photokeratitis and cataracts; Class 3B+ lasers hazardous

label: Blue Light
description: Blue light (450–495 nm) is scattered most strongly by the atmosphere, creating the blue sky color. It stimulates the circadian clock through ipRGC (intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells) sensitive at ~480 nm. Blue LEDs (Nakamura, Nobel Prize 2014) enabled white-LED lighting and displays.
interactions: Rayleigh scattering produces blue sky and twilight
circadian rhythm disruption via melanopsin at 480 nm
short depth of focus in eye (chromatic aberration)
applications: blue LED room lighting (phosphor-converted to white)
hazards: blue light hazard (photochemical retinal damage) from high-intensity sources; screen blue light debated for sleep disruption

label: Cyan Light
description: Cyan (495–520 nm) is perceived as a blue-green mixture by the eye's S and M cones. It corresponds to the peak absorption of the retinal photopigment melanopsin (~480 nm), important for circadian regulation. Cyan is also the complementary color to red and plays a key role in CMY printing.
applications: cyan laser (488 nm Argon laser, flow cytometry)
hazards: retinal photochemical hazard from high-intensity cyan lasers

label: Green Light
description: Green (520–565 nm) is where the human eye is most sensitive under photopic (daylight) conditions — peak luminous efficiency at 555 nm. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue, reflecting green, which is why plants appear green. The 532 nm DPSS green laser is ubiquitous in pointers and alignment tools.
interactions: peak photopic luminous efficiency of human eye (555 nm)
strong LiDAR signal return from vegetation
applications: green laser pointers (532 nm DPSS Nd:YAG 2nd harmonic)
night-vision display phosphors (P1, P31 phosphors 525 nm)
hazards: green laser pointer injuries to pilots and eyes documented; Class 3R and above are regulated

label: Yellow Light
description: Yellow (565–590 nm) is produced by the additive mixture of red and green light, or by excitation of the retina's M-cone. Sodium vapor streetlamps emit characteristic yellow doublet lines at 589.0 and 589.6 nm. Yellow is used in warning signs due to high visibility and contrast against dark backgrounds.
interactions: perceived by M- and L-cone overlap
high scotopic visibility near twilight (Purkinje shift)
strong visual contrast against dark backgrounds
sodium D-line doublet 589.0/589.6 nm from sodium vapor
applications: medical ophthalmic lasers (yellow 577 nm for retinal treatment)
hazards: no special hazard beyond standard photochemical limits

label: Orange Light
description: Orange (590–625 nm) stimulates both M and L cones but not S cones. It is used in road safety (orange traffic cones, hazard lights) and is the color of flame combustion at moderate temperatures (~1200 °C). Orange He-Ne laser lines and neon signs produce saturated orange-red emission.
interactions: associated with carotenoid pigments (carrots, autumn leaves)
high visibility in fog and low-light conditions
applications: high-visibility safety clothing and road signs
sunset sky color from Mie scattering
hazards: no special hazard at normal intensities
sources: incandescent filaments (blackbody ~2800 K peak near orange)

label: Red Light
description: Red (625–750 nm) has the longest wavelength visible to humans, stimulating only the L-cone. It is least scattered by the atmosphere, making it ideal for long-range signaling (traffic lights, aircraft lights). The first laser ever operated was a ruby laser at 694.3 nm in 1960.
interactions: minimal Rayleigh scattering — long range signaling
deep tissue penetration (~1–2 cm) for photobiomodulation
absorbed by hemoglobin and water beyond 700 nm
applications: red traffic signals and aircraft anticollision lights
hazards: Class 3B and 4 red lasers can cause permanent retinal injury; no ionizing hazard

label: UVA — Near UV
description: UVA (315–400 nm) constitutes ~95% of UV reaching the Earth's surface. It penetrates glass and induces tanning by oxidizing existing melanin. UVA causes photoaging and contributes to skin cancer risk. Blacklights (365 nm) excite fluorescent materials. EPROM erasure uses 253.7 nm but UVA at 365 nm is used in some exposure systems.
interactions: generates reactive oxygen species in skin
applications: UV curing of adhesives and inks
hazards: contributes to photoaging, cataracts, and melanoma risk with chronic exposure; not acutely ionizing but damages DNA via indirect ROS mechanism

label: UVB — Mid UV
description: UVB (280–315 nm) is partially blocked by the ozone layer. It directly damages DNA by forming cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs), causing sunburn and increasing skin cancer risk. Paradoxically, UVB is essential for vitamin D3 synthesis in skin. The UV Index is primarily a UVB metric.
interactions: induces vitamin D3 synthesis in skin (295–310 nm)
applications: phototherapy for psoriasis (311 nm narrowband UVB)
hazards: primary cause of sunburn; direct DNA mutagenic; elevated skin cancer (basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma) risk; photokeratitis (snow blindness)
sources: sun (filtered by ozone; increases with altitude and latitude)

label: UVC — Far UV / Germicidal
description: UVC (100–280 nm) is almost entirely absorbed by atmospheric ozone and does not reach Earth's surface naturally. Germicidal UV at 253.7 nm (mercury lamp) inactivates bacteria, viruses, and mold by direct DNA/RNA damage. Far-UVC at 222 nm (KrCl excimer) is being studied as a safer germicidal alternative.
interactions: completely absorbed by atmospheric ozone above 280 nm
direct DNA/RNA photolesion formation at 253.7 nm
ozone generation from O2 photolysis at wavelengths below 242 nm
Lyman-alpha line 121.6 nm in solar EUV
hazards: ionizing to biological molecules; severe photokeratitis and erythema (sunburn) in seconds; corneal damage; potential carcinogen at high doses; NEVER use without proper eye and skin protection

label: Soft X-rays
description: Soft X-rays (0.1–10 nm, 0.1–10 keV) interact with matter primarily via the photoelectric effect and are attenuated by centimeters of tissue. They are used in mammography, airport security backscatter scanners, and extreme UV (EUV) lithography at 13.5 nm for chip manufacturing. Water-window X-rays (2.3–4.4 nm) enable bio-imaging in liquid.
interactions: photoelectric absorption dominates at low keV
zone-plate X-ray microscopy achieves <50 nm resolution
hazards: ionizing radiation; damages DNA; stochastic cancer risk; ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) principle applies; lead shielding required

label: Hard X-rays
description: Hard X-rays (0.001–0.1 nm, 10 keV–300 keV) penetrate deeply into matter and are used in medical CT scanners (30–140 kVp), chest radiography, and industrial non-destructive testing. Compton scattering becomes the dominant interaction mechanism above ~100 keV. Pair production begins near 1.022 MeV.
interactions: photoelectric effect at lower keV edge
deep tissue penetration (cm to cm in lead required for shielding)
hazards: ionizing; deterministic effects (radiation burns) at high doses; stochastic (cancer) risk; cumulative dose tracked via dosimetry badges; lead apron required for occupational workers

label: Medical Gamma Rays
description: Medical gamma rays (30 EHz–3 ZHz, 10 keV–10 MeV) are emitted by radionuclides used in nuclear medicine. Cobalt-60 emits gamma at 1.17 and 1.33 MeV, used in Gamma Knife radiosurgery. PET scanners detect 511 keV annihilation photons from fluorine-18 (F-18 FDG). Tc-99m (140 keV) is the most widely used diagnostic isotope.
interactions: deep penetration requiring dense shielding (lead, concrete)
applications: radiation therapy linear accelerators (6–18 MeV photons)
hazards: highly ionizing; deterministic effects above ~1 Gy (radiation sickness, burns, hair loss); stochastic cancer risk; thick lead or concrete shielding required; occupational limits 50 mSv/year (ICRP)

label: High-Energy Gamma / Cosmic Gamma
description: High-energy gamma rays (>300 ZHz, >10 MeV) originate from cosmic events: supernovae, neutron star mergers, gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), and particle physics experiments. They initiate electromagnetic cascades in the atmosphere detected by Cherenkov telescopes (H.E.S.S., MAGIC). Pair production in electric fields of nuclei is the dominant interaction.
interactions: pair production dominant (e⁺e⁻ pair creation in nuclear Coulomb field)
Cherenkov radiation from ultra-relativistic shower particles
cosmic gamma rays observed via atmospheric air showers
hazards: extremely ionizing; no terrestrial natural source above background; hazardous near particle accelerators and nuclear devices; no natural terrestrial exposure

label: Infrasound
description: Infrasound (<20 Hz) propagates as longitudinal pressure waves in air or water over vast distances with very low attenuation. Earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, large explosions, and ocean surf generate infrasound monitored by the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO). Whales communicate in infrasound over hundreds of kilometers.
interactions: extremely long propagation distances with low attenuation
resonates with body cavities (eye, sinus) at 12–20 Hz
hazards: exposure to high-SPL infrasound (>120 dB SPL) can cause disorientation, nausea, and resonance effects in internal organs; normal environmental levels not hazardous

label: Audible Sound
description: Audible sound (20 Hz–20 kHz) is the range of human hearing. It propagates as longitudinal pressure waves at ~343 m/s in air. Speech occupies 300 Hz–3.4 kHz; music spans 20 Hz–20 kHz; sonar uses focused pulses. Hearing sensitivity peaks near 3–4 kHz due to ear canal resonance.
interactions: longitudinal pressure wave propagation in air (~343 m/s)
applications: acoustic guitar and piano (88 keys: 27.5 Hz–4186 Hz)
hazards: prolonged exposure above 85 dB SPL causes noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL); OSHA limits 90 dB for 8 hours; impulse noise above 140 dB SPL causes immediate damage

label: Ultrasound
description: Ultrasound (>20 kHz) is used in medical imaging (2–18 MHz), industrial NDT (flaw detection), bat echolocation (20–200 kHz), and ultrasonic cleaning. Higher frequencies give better spatial resolution but shorter penetration depth in tissue. Therapeutic ultrasound (physiotherapy) uses ~1 MHz; HIFU (high-intensity focused ultrasound) ablates tissue.
interactions: attenuation increases with frequency (higher resolution, shorter range)
reflection at acoustic impedance boundaries (tissue interfaces)
Doppler shift used for blood flow velocity
applications: medical diagnostic ultrasound (2–18 MHz B-mode and Doppler)
hazards: diagnostic levels non-hazardous (MI < 1.9, TI < 6); high-intensity therapeutic/surgical ultrasound can heat or ablate tissue; industrial cavitation can cause surface pitting
